identity.real_world_identity_notes: The AC mod content 'wsc_legends_shelby_daytona' (WSC Legends 60's Pack, Team WSC Legends, formerly distributed as part of 'Bazza's & AC Legends GTR' mod pack) is a third-party physics/model recreation, not official Kunos content. It represents the Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe: a special aerodynamic body designed by Peter Brock, fitted to the leaf-spring chassis and running gear of the AC/Shelby Cobra 289 Mark II under FIA Appendix J's post-homologation special-body freedom (the same freedom that shaped the Ferrari 250 GTO and Jaguar Low Drag E-Type). Six were built for the 1964-1965 World Championship for Makes: the first (CSX2287) by Shelby's own team in Venice, California; the remaining five (CSX2286, CSX2299, CSX2300, CSX2601, CSX2602) by Carrozzeria Gransport in Modena, Italy. The chassis itself was manufactured in England by AC Cars Ltd and exported to Shelby for engine/gearbox fitting and finishing, so 'AC' identifies the chassis manufacturer, not the racing marque under which the car is known and was campaigned.

Wikipedia's Shelby Daytona article and a specialist FIA historic-racing eligibility guide (historicmotorsportcentral.com) independently agree on the six-chassis production run, the two build locations, and the Appendix J homologation-freedom origin of the special body. The AC Cobra Wikipedia article separately confirms AC Cars Ltd as the chassis manufacturer and the shared Cobra Mark II leaf-spring platform. A repository scan found no existing curated record for this car.

claims.basis: Wikipedia's Shelby Daytona article and a specialist FIA historic-racing eligibility guide (historicmotorsportcentral.com) independently agree on the six-chassis production run, the two build locations, and the Appendix J homologation-freedom origin of the special body. The AC Cobra Wikipedia article separately confirms AC Cars Ltd as the chassis manufacturer and the shared Cobra Mark II leaf-spring platform. A repository scan found no existing curated record for this car.

Two independent specification sources agree the Daytona Coupe used a four-speed Borg-Warner T10 manual transmission. A dedicated technical history of the Borg-Warner T-10 explicitly states all four forward speeds were synchronized, and the same T10 model is independently confirmed as this car's transmission. The Borg-Warner T10 is a conventional floor-shifted manual, and the specialist FIA eligibility guide confirms period cars used the standard (non-Hurst) shift linkage rather than any sequential or paddle system. The reviewed sources did not establish the remaining technique and wheel fields, which stay unknown in the real-car baseline: /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/integrated_display, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/open_top, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/shape, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/shift_lights, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/throttle_lift, /authentic_controls/transmission/shift_pattern, /authentic_controls/transmission/standing_start_clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/clutch, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/manual_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/throttle_lift.
